clue.text: They can be a bit of a trial in whodunits

definitions.text: They can be a bit of a trial in whodunits

parts.words: They can be a bit of a trial in whodunits
parts.note: reads as complaining that some scenes drag in detective stories, but means the places where a trial is held, a regular setting in mystery fiction

explanation.surface: A reader grumbles that some chapters of detective novels are tedious.
explanation.definitionFit: Murder mysteries often end with a judge and jury, so the rooms of a law court host part of the trial.

clue.text: Unconscious state of Robin Cook

explanation.surface: A writer is pictured lying senseless.
explanation.definitionFit: A deep loss of consciousness has this name, which is also the title of Robin Cook's 1977 medical thriller.

clue.text: The major one's up north, right in America

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the letters for America

parts.words: America
parts.note: USA is the common abbreviation for the United States of America

parts.words: right

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a major figure has moved north and is now settled in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points at the Great Bear constellation, Ursa Major, seen in northern skies; 'in' puts R inside USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is the major constellation of the bear pair, high in the northern sky.

clue.text: He was at pains, perhaps, in play

definitions.text: He was at pains, perhaps, in play

parts.words: He was at pains, perhaps, in play
parts.note: someone at pains takes care, so a title character who takes care stars in a Pinter drama

explanation.surface: A man made a great effort during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Harold Pinter's 1960 play has this title; 'at pains' means taking care, so its hero is literally a care-taker.
explanation.definitionFit: A person at pains is careful, a taker of care, and Pinter's play is named for such a custodian.

clue.text: Daggers drawn from wardrobe, lifelike replicas for Scottish play

indicators.note: drawn from says the letters are pulled out of the run of the next words, as a dagger is drawn

parts.words: wardrobe, lifelike

explanation.surface: Prop daggers for a production of Macbeth are taken out of the costume store, convincingly realistic.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Scottish play' is Macbeth, which actors avoid naming; its famous dagger scene is pure surface here.
explanation.definitionFit: Obelus, plural obeli, is the printers' dagger mark used for footnotes.

clue.text: "Paving with fire the sky and the floods " (Shelley)

definitions.text: "Paving with fire the sky and the floods " (Shelley)

parts.words: "Paving with fire the sky and the floods " (Shelley)
parts.note: a line by Shelley with one word missing before floods; the gap is filled by an adjective meaning like marble

explanation.surface: A Romantic poet's line about fire lighting up the sky over the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing epithet means marble-like, describing waters smooth and gleaming as polished stone.

clue.text: French attitude includes inconsequential dialogue

indicators.note: includes says the answer is held within the run of the words French attitude

parts.words: French attitude

explanation.surface: A French manner of speaking involves trivial conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: Light, unimportant talk is idle conversation.

clue.text: As long as a line of As You Like It? It's two feet longer!

definitions.text: As long as a line of As You Like It? It's two feet longer!

parts.words: As long as a line of As You Like It? It's two feet longer!
parts.note: Shakespeare's verse lines have five metrical feet; add two more and you get a seven-foot line

explanation.surface: Someone compares the length of a Shakespeare line with something two feet longer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'feet' tempts a measure of length; here it means metrical feet, so pentameter plus two.
explanation.definitionFit: A verse line of seven metrical feet carries this name, two more than Shakespeare's usual pentameter.

clue.text: A bit lucky, perhaps, for Half Sixpence

definitions.text: A bit lucky, perhaps, for Half Sixpence

parts.words: A bit lucky, perhaps, for Half Sixpence
parts.note: an old British coin worth half of sixpence was a bit of this name, and its number is often called lucky

explanation.surface: Someone thinks the musical Half Sixpence had a stroke of luck.
explanation.walkthrough: Half Sixpence is a British musical; half of sixpence is the old coin called a 'bit', and three is a lucky number.
explanation.definitionFit: The pre-decimal British coin worth three old pence was half a sixpence.

clue.text: They were accustomed to handling smooth bores

definitions.text: They were accustomed to handling smooth bores

parts.words: They were accustomed to handling smooth bores
parts.note: seems to be about putting up with suave dullards, but smooth bores are unrifled gun barrels carried by old soldiers

explanation.surface: Some people were used to dealing with polished but tedious company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bores' wants to be tiresome people; it means gun barrels, and the musket was a smoothbore weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers armed with the smoothbore musket were named for the weapon they carried.

clue.text: Thus clinging fast to that slight within her arms, the mother drifted out…" (Dombey and Son)

definitions.text: Thus clinging fast to that slight within her arms, the mother drifted out…" (Dombey and Son)

parts.words: Thus clinging fast to that slight within her arms, the mother drifted out…" (Dombey and Son)
parts.note: a Dickens deathbed line with one word missing after slight; the gap is a thin pole such as a mast that a drowning person clings to

explanation.surface: A Dickens passage about a dying mother holding her child.
explanation.definitionFit: A slender pole such as a mast is what Dickens likens the frail child to, something to cling to at sea.

clue.text: Keith Richards, say, as portrayed by O. Henry?

explanation.surface: A rock guitarist is described as he might appear in an American short story.
explanation.walkthrough: Keith Richards plays in the band; O. Henry ran a humorous weekly with this title, and a collection of his stories is named Rolling Stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Richards is a member of the famous band, and the title was used by O. Henry for his 1890s comic paper.

clue.text: Awful or asocial yen in gambling venue (6)

indicators.note: awful suggests something done badly, so the following letters are jumbled

parts.words: or asocial yen

explanation.surface: A dreadful, unsociable longing seizes someone at a casino.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray '(6)' in the clue is a printing slip. The anagram also gives Ian Fleming's first Bond novel, set at the gambling house it names.
explanation.definitionFit: A casino is a gaming house, and Fleming's fictional casino at Royale-les-Eaux is one.

clue.text: An intruder in the works of D. H. Lawrence

definitions.text: the works of D. H. Lawrence

explanation.surface: Someone uninvited is found among Lawrence's writings.
explanation.definitionFit: A person entering land without permission is an intruder, and Lawrence wrote a 1912 novel titled after one.

clue.text: One way of keeping busy at Trevor Griffiths's Big House

explanation.surface: A playwright's large home offers ways to stay busy.
explanation.walkthrough: Trevor Griffiths is a British playwright; his play Occupations concerns the 1920 seizure of factories in Turin.
explanation.definitionFit: A job or pastime keeps one busy; seizing a building such as a factory is also this.

clue.text: Choice Proustian quest

explanation.surface: A reader picks Proust's long search for lost time.
explanation.walkthrough: Proust's novel is A la recherche du temps perdu, In Search of Lost Time.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means exquisite or select, and the French noun means search, as in Proust's title.

clue.text: His 14 may lead him to Muriel Spark's 1970 novel

definitions.text: His 14 may lead him to Muriel Spark's 1970 novel

parts.words: His 14 may lead him to Muriel Spark's 1970 novel
parts.note: the job from the entry numbered 14 puts a man in the place named by Spark's book, The Driver's Seat

explanation.surface: A man's career path brings him to a particular Muriel Spark book.
explanation.walkthrough: 14 refers to the answer at 14-down, a job; Muriel Spark's 1970 novel is The Driver's Seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A paid driver of a private car sits in the driver's seat as his work.

clue.text: The subject is a town in Belgium

explanation.surface: Someone announces that the topic under discussion is a Belgian town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subject' means a vassal, not a topic.
explanation.definitionFit: A feudal vassal owing allegiance is called this, and it is also the name of a Belgian city on the Meuse.

clue.text: American composer puts French money on French company

indicators.note: on here means the first piece comes before the second in the across answer

parts.words: French money
parts.note: a sou was an old French coin

parts.words: French company
parts.note: SA, societe anonyme, is the French abbreviation for a limited company

explanation.surface: A US musician invests euros in a firm based in France.
explanation.walkthrough: John Philip Sousa was the American march king.
explanation.definitionFit: John Philip Sousa wrote marches such as The Stars and Stripes Forever.

clue.text: "With shoulders fit to bear The weight of mightiest monarchies " (Paradise Lost)

definitions.text: "With shoulders fit to bear The weight of mightiest monarchies " (Paradise Lost)

parts.words: "With shoulders fit to bear The weight of mightiest monarchies " (Paradise Lost)
parts.note: a Milton line with one word missing before shoulders; the gap is an adjective from the Titan who held up the heavens

explanation.surface: Milton describes Beelzebub as broad-shouldered enough to carry empires.
explanation.definitionFit: Like the Titan Atlas, who bore the sky, the epithet means strong enough to carry a great load.

clue.text: Board meeting reported by Eliot (1,4, 5)

parts.words: Board meeting reported by Eliot
parts.note: seems to be minutes of a company board, but means an encounter on a chequered board, the title of part II of The Waste Land

explanation.surface: Eliot writes up the minutes of a company board meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray '(1,4, 5)' is a printing slip. T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land has a section with this title.
explanation.definitionFit: A contest between two players over a chequered board is a match of the royal game.

clue.text: An orphan in The Idiot

indicators.note: in says the answer sits within the letters of the words that follow

parts.words: The Idiot

explanation.surface: An orphaned character appears in Dostoevsky's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Johanna Spyri's Swiss girl lives with her grandfather after losing her parents.

clue.text: Half of a 2X offering by Roald Dahl

definitions.text: Half of a 2X offering by Roald Dahl

parts.words: Half of a 2X offering by Roald Dahl
parts.note: two Xs are two smooches at the end of a letter, and Dahl's story collection repeats the word once for each

explanation.surface: A fraction of something doubled is presented by Roald Dahl.
explanation.walkthrough: Roald Dahl's 1960 collection is Kiss Kiss; an X stands for one at the end of a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An X at the foot of a letter stands for a peck on the lips, and Dahl's title doubles it.

clue.text: With which the sea might see, thought Marie Corelli

definitions.text: With which the sea might see, thought Marie Corelli

parts.words: With which the sea might see, thought Marie Corelli
parts.note: the organs of sight, here imagined belonging to the ocean, as in a fanciful phrase of the Victorian novelist

explanation.surface: A popular novelist imagines the ocean being able to look about.
explanation.definitionFit: The organs of vision are what anything, even an ocean, would need in order to see.

clue.text: Dispatch Forrester's vessel

explanation.surface: Someone sends off a novelist's boat.
explanation.walkthrough: C. S. Forester (printed here Forrester) wrote the 1943 novel The Ship.
explanation.definitionFit: To send goods off is to consign them, and a seagoing vessel was the subject of Forester's wartime novel.

clue.text: One setting for the Deighton Set

definitions.text: One setting for the Deighton Set

parts.words: One setting for the Deighton Set
parts.note: Len Deighton's spy trilogy Game, Set and Match has a middle novel titled after a Latin American capital plus Set

explanation.surface: A location is chosen for a group of people around a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Len Deighton's trilogy is Berlin Game, Mexico Set, London Match.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mexican capital is where much of Deighton's Mexico Set takes place.

clue.text: It is associated with the book by Browning

definitions.text: It is associated with the book by Browning

parts.words: It is associated with the book by Browning
parts.note: Robert Browning's long poem is titled with a circlet joined to The Book

explanation.surface: Something is linked to a volume written by Browning.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Browning's verse novel is The Ring and the Book.
explanation.definitionFit: A circlet, in Browning's title, is paired with the Book.

clue.text: British women creating a precedent in holy orders?

definitions.text: British women creating a precedent in holy orders?

parts.words: British women creating a precedent in holy orders?
parts.note: looks like modern women being ordained, but means female priests of the ancient Celtic religion of Britain

explanation.surface: Women in Britain break new ground by being ordained as priests.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests women priests in the Church; the answer is the priestesses of the ancient Britons, who long predate them.
explanation.definitionFit: Female priests of the pre-Christian Celtic religion held sacred office in ancient Britain.
